subject.question: How can a historical astronomical model be written so that its geometry, its values, its position and the reasoning about it stay apart and each can be checked?

subject.work: Ptolemy's solar model, in its eccentric and its epicyclic form, as Noel Swerdlow uses it in The Renaissance of Astronomy (2026), chapter 1

subject.method: The language astra/1 writes a model, its parametrisations, a superposition, figures and derivations as texts of their own kinds, each with its own check. The case study writes eighteen such texts from Swerdlow's pages on Ptolemy's solar model and reports what the checks found.
limits: A derivation that passes the four checks is not a formal proof in an axiomatic system: truth is tested on samples, rules are matched as schemas, configuration conditions are evaluated numerically.
Cases have to be found by the author of a derivation; the checks do not propose the distinction.
Hypotheses have to fix a parameter; inequalities between parameters and hypotheses of incidence are not supported.
The grades 'read off the construction' and 'calculation' are tested numerically and not replayed symbolically; an expansion is tested at three sizes of the small ratio.
The language is planar; motions taken from tables are not implemented; only the solar model is written.
The level 'attested' checks that a source is named, not that it says what the parametrisation says.
The Almagest is not among the addressable texts; the attribution to Ptolemy and the loci in the Almagest are as Swerdlow's page gives them.
The propositions of Euclid are cited by the page of Heath's translation, not by paragraph.
The code is not yet public.

claims.text: A model is the pure geometry and holds no values; a parametrisation gives the parameters values, each with a source or a stated gap, and one model has many.

The diagram that shows both forms of Ptolemy's solar model is a superposition, and their equivalence is the conclusion of a derivation in it under hypotheses on the radii: in position when R′ = R and r = e, in direction when R′/r = R/e.

The parallelogram argument by Elements I.28 and I.33 does not apply at the apsides, κ̄ = 0° and κ̄ = 180°, where the points O, E, S and C lie on the apsidal line; the derivation therefore argues by three cases: off the apsidal line, at the apogee, at the perigee.

Four questions are asked of a derivation, each presupposing the one before: whether it is grounded, whether every proposition is true, whether every step is justified by the rule it names, and whether it is conclusive.
claims.gap: A definition of the language; the specification (spec/astra-1.md) has no fr: address in the issue.

claims.text: The largest equation of centre under Ptolemy's values is 2;23°, as printed; under al-Battānī's values it is 1;59,9°, and the page reports 1;59,10°.

Ptolemy's reported eccentricity and apogee, 2;29,30 and 65;30°, follow from his rounded arcs of mean motion, to within what a computation with a table of chords loses, and not from the day counts of the seasons.
claims.gap: The issue names the printed page (p. 22) beside the determination but no fr: address; Ptolemy's steps are not on the page, and Almagest III 4 is not available in addressable form.

claims.text: Every astra text and every part of it has an address beginning with fr:, down to a value with its source and a step of a derivation.

agent.summary: Description of astra/1, a language that writes a historical astronomical model as texts of separate kinds: model (geometry without values), parametrisation (values with sources), superposition, figure, derivation. The case is Ptolemy's solar model in its eccentric and epicyclic form as Noel Swerdlow uses it in The Renaissance of Astronomy (2026). The models are attributed to Ptolemy, Swerdlow's pages are the witness, the astra texts are the author's. A derivation that passes the four checks is not a formal proof: truth is tested on samples.
answers: What are model, parametrisation, state, superposition, figure and derivation in astra/1, and which statements belong to each?
What do the levels of the checks mean for each kind of text?
Under which hypotheses are the eccentric and the epicyclic form of Ptolemy's solar model equivalent, and in what?
By which steps and rules is the equivalence derived, and where does the parallelogram argument not apply?
How are the equation of centre and its maximum derived and computed in the eccentric model?
What address does a part of an astra text have?
How does astra/1 differ in its design aims from GCLC, Eukleides, Cinderella, GeoGebra, JSXGraph and Duke's animations?

terms.meaning: the pure geometry: parameter symbols, a kinematic variable, a construction without coordinates, observables; it holds no values
a set of values for a model's parameters, each with the place where it stands and with the name of whose values they are
a state is a value of the kinematic variable; a model under a parametrisation in a state is a configuration
several models placed in one plane with their inputs identified; it adds no geometry
geometrical reasoning in a model or a superposition: hypotheses, auxiliary constructions, propositions derived from named premises by named rules, quantities computed or determined, a conclusion
whose model or whose values it is; the address of the text whose use of the model is analysed; who wrote the astra text
equivalence is a relation between two models relative to hypotheses and to what is compared (position or direction); two texts are the same model when they are the same geometry up to renaming
a number that is zero when a proposition holds
what a rule takes from the figure; a state in which such a condition fails, so that the rule does not apply there
a given that a proposition needs and that is not cited on the way to it
level of a parametrisation: every value has a source or a stated gap; it checks that a source is named, not that it says what the parametrisation says

do_not: Do not name Swerdlow as the author of the models: the models are Ptolemy's, Swerdlow's pages are the witness.
Do not present a derivation that passes the four checks as a formal proof.
Do not attribute the derivation of the equation of centre to the witness: it is supplied by the author of the astra text.
Do not take the drawing values of a figure for attested values.
Do not treat equivalence as identity: the eccentric and the epicyclic form are different models.
Do not read the level 'attested' as a confirmation that the source says what the parametrisation says.
Do not cite the loci in the Almagest as checked: they are as Swerdlow's page gives them.

title: astra/1
subtitle: A Language for Historical Astronomical Models and the Geometrical Reasoning about Them
abstract: A historical astronomical model is a geometrical construction with a kinematic variable. Texts about such models do four things at once: they describe a geometry, give it numbers, show it in one position, and reason about it. We present astra/1, a small language that writes each of the four as a text of its own kind. A model is the pure geometry: parameter symbols, a kinematic variable, a construction without coordinates, observables; it holds no values. A parametrisation gives the parameters values, each with the page it comes from; one model has many. A state is a value of the kinematic variable; model, parametrisation and state together give a configuration. A superposition places several models in one plane and identifies their inputs. A derivation is the operation that follows construction: hypotheses, auxiliary constructions, propositions derived from named premises by named rules, quantities computed or determined, a conclusion. Four questions are asked of a derivation: whether it is grounded, whether every proposition is true, whether every step is an instance of the rule it names with its configuration conditions holding, and whether the conclusion rests on what is cited. Every text names three roles that must not be confused: whose model it is, which text's use of it is analysed, and who wrote the description. We describe Ptolemy's solar model, in its eccentric and its epicyclic form, as Noel Swerdlow uses it in The Renaissance of Astronomy (2026). The diagram that shows both forms is a superposition, and their equivalence is the conclusion of a derivation under hypotheses on the radii: equivalence in position when the radii are equal, by Elements I.28 and I.33, and in direction when they are proportional, by VI.6 and I.29. The parallelogram argument does not apply at the apsides, where the parallelogram collapses; the derivation therefore argues by three cases. Ptolemy's reported eccentricity and apogee follow from his rounded arcs of mean motion, not from the day counts of the seasons.
